title: “Can You Lust After Someone You Love and Still Call It Pure?”
paragraphs:
“Can You Lust After Someone You Love and Still Call It Pure?”
When Desire Feels Like Love… But Heaven Sees Something Else
It didn’t start as something dark.

It started with admiration… a glance that lingered just a second too long, a thought that felt harmless because it came wrapped in affection. You told yourself, “I love them.” And maybe you do. Maybe your heart really does care. Maybe you would protect them, provide for them, stand beside them in the daylight.
But what happens in the quiet?
What happens when no one sees the thoughts that begin to shape how you look at them… how you imagine them… how you want them?
Because somewhere between love and longing, something shifts.
And Jesus didn’t stay silent about that shift.
He looked straight through behavior and pierced intention when He said, in Matthew 5:28:
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
In the Greek, He didn’t use a soft word.
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn)
“to desire her… to crave her… to set the heart upon possessing her.”
This wasn’t about noticing beauty.
This was about the heart deciding, “I want this for myself.”
Even if you call it love.
Even if you wrap it in commitment.
Even if you say, “But they’re mine” or “I plan to marry them.”
Because heaven doesn’t measure purity by your labels.
It measures it by your posture.
And this is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because you can love someone… and still reduce them.
You can care deeply… and still objectify quietly.
You can speak kindly… and still imagine them in ways that dishonor who they are in God’s eyes.
That tension you feel right now?
That’s conviction, not condemnation.
Because Scripture never separates love from holiness.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5, Paul writes:
The phrase “passion of lust” in Greek is:
πάθει ἐπιθυμίας (pathei epithymias)
A burning… consuming desire that controls rather than honors.
So let’s be honest.
If your “love” is driven by a need to consume rather than to honor…
Is it still love?
Or is it something wearing love’s face?
Because biblical love never begins with taking.
It begins with surrender.
The kind of love Jesus showed wasn’t driven by desire to possess—it was driven by willingness to sacrifice.
And that’s where most people struggle.
Because lust says, “I want.”
But love says, “I protect.”
Lust says, “They satisfy me.”
But love says, “I will not use them, even in my thoughts.”
Lust says, “No one will know.”
But love says, “God already sees.”
Hebrew gives us another layer.
In the Old Testament, the word for pure—טָהוֹר (tahor)—means clean, uncontaminated, untouched by mixture.
Not partially clean.
Not mostly clean.
Unmixed.
So here’s the question that hits deeper than comfort:
Can something be called pure if it’s mixed with hidden desire that dishonors?
That’s not meant to shame you.
It’s meant to wake you up.
Because this isn’t about losing love.
It’s about rescuing it.
Real love is worth protecting from distortion.
Real love refuses to turn a person into a private fantasy.
Real love fears God more than it craves gratification.
And if you’re reading this and realizing your heart hasn’t been clean…
You’re not disqualified.
You’re being invited.
Because Jesus didn’t expose hearts to destroy them.
He exposed them so He could rewrite them.
That’s the Gospel.
That even the thoughts you’re ashamed of… the patterns you’ve normalized… the desires you’ve justified…
They don’t have the final word.
Grace does.
But grace never leaves you unchanged.
It calls you higher.
It calls you to see people the way heaven sees them.
Not as objects.
Not as outlets.
But as souls.
Sit in it.
Let it speak.
Be honest.
Someone else reading your honesty might finally stop hiding too.
It’s a daily decision.
And if you want to go deeper—if you’re serious about walking in purity, understanding Scripture in its original depth, and letting God reshape how you love—stay close.
Follow.
Because truth like this isn’t popular, but it’s necessary.
It’s partnership in the Gospel.
It’s choosing to glorify God with your reach, your voice, your influence.
If your heart is hungry for more than surface-level faith… this is where you stay.
Because one day you’ll realize…
It was never just about controlling desire.
It was about becoming someone who loves the way Christ loves.
And that changes everything.
